questions.prompt: What does calling task.cancel() on a running Swift task do immediately?

options.text: It sets the isCancelled flag to true on the task and its child tasks.
options.explanation: Calling cancel() sets the cancellation flag and propagates it down the task tree.

options.text: It immediately kills the underlying operating system POSIX thread.
options.explanation: Swift cancellation is cooperative and does not kill threads.

options.text: It resets all state variables in the enclosing view controller to nil.
options.explanation: Task cancellation affects task state, not view controller properties.

options.text: It forces the current function to return an empty default value.
options.explanation: Code continues running until it cooperatively checks for cancellation.

questions.prompt: Which property returns a Boolean indicating whether the current task was cancelled?

options.text: Task.hasAborted
options.explanation: hasAborted is not a property on Swift Task.

options.text: Task.isCancelled
options.explanation: Task.isCancelled returns true if the current task has received a cancellation request.

options.text: Task.isInterrupted
options.explanation: isInterrupted does not exist in Swift concurrency.

options.text: Task.shouldStop
options.explanation: shouldStop is not a Swift concurrency API property.

questions.prompt: What does try Task.checkCancellation() do when a task has received a cancellation request?

options.text: It restarts the task from the beginning with reduced priority.
options.explanation: Swift does not restart cancelled tasks automatically.

options.text: It returns false to indicate execution should halt immediately.
options.explanation: checkCancellation() throws an error rather than returning a Boolean.

options.text: It throws a CancellationError immediately to unwind the call stack.
options.explanation: Calling checkCancellation() throws CancellationError if isCancelled is true.

options.text: It raises a fatal assertion failure in debug scheme configurations.
options.explanation: Cancellation is a normal runtime condition and does not trigger fatal assertions.

questions.prompt: Why is Swift task cancellation termed cooperative?

options.text: Because multiple tasks share a single cooperative memory cache.
options.explanation: Cooperative cancellation relates to execution flow, not caching.

options.text: Because tasks can only be cancelled by other tasks on the same thread.
options.explanation: Tasks can be cancelled from any thread or actor context.

options.text: Because child tasks vote on whether to accept a cancellation request.
options.explanation: Cancellation cascades automatically; child tasks do not vote on cancellation.

options.text: Because code must inspect cancellation flags and stop running voluntarily.
options.explanation: Swift does not forcibly terminate threads; running code must cooperate by checking flags.

questions.prompt: What happens if a heavy CPU loop never checks Task.isCancelled or checkCancellation()?

options.text: The loop continues running to completion, wasting CPU and battery.
options.explanation: Without cooperative checks, running loops do not stop when cancelled.

options.text: Swift terminates the app process with an unhandled exception.
options.explanation: Unchecked tasks continue running normally without crashing.

options.text: The thread execution speed slows down to zero instructions per second.
options.explanation: The thread continues executing at its scheduled priority.

options.text: The compiler refuses to compile the loop under Swift 6 mode.
options.explanation: Checking cancellation is a runtime responsibility, not a compiler error.

questions.prompt: How does the SwiftUI .task modifier behave when a view disappears from the screen?

options.text: It keeps the task active indefinitely until the application terminates.
options.explanation: The task modifier cancels tasks on disappearance to prevent leaks.

options.text: It automatically cancels the running task when the view disappears.
options.explanation: The SwiftUI .task modifier automatically cancels its task upon view disappearance.

options.text: It converts the task into a detached background maintenance task.
options.explanation: The task is cancelled, not detached into maintenance.

options.text: It forces synchronous completion of the task before view teardown.
options.explanation: SwiftUI cancels tasks asynchronously without blocking the UI thread.

questions.prompt: How does Task.sleep behave when its enclosing task is cancelled during sleep?

options.text: It ignores cancellation and completes the full sleep duration.
options.explanation: Task.sleep is cancellation-aware and will not sleep its full duration.

options.text: It returns false to indicate the sleep was interrupted early.
options.explanation: Task.sleep throws CancellationError rather than returning a Boolean.

options.text: It wakes up immediately and throws CancellationError to the caller.
options.explanation: Task.sleep detects cancellation, aborts its sleep timer, and throws CancellationError.

options.text: It resets the device hardware clock to synchronize with NTP.
options.explanation: Task.sleep is a software scheduler timer, not a hardware clock reset.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid presenting error alerts when catching CancellationError?

options.text: Because CancellationError crashes UIAlertController when displayed.
options.explanation: CancellationError is a standard Swift error and does not crash UI.

options.text: Because presenting alerts re-enables the cancelled background task.
options.explanation: Alert presentations do not resume or re-enable cancelled tasks.

options.text: Because CancellationError is erased by the compiler in release builds.
options.explanation: CancellationError exists and behaves identically in debug and release builds.

options.text: Because cancellation is usually intentional when users navigate away.
options.explanation: Presenting alerts for intentional navigation confuses users with bogus error popups.

questions.prompt: Which construct guarantees cleanup code runs when a task exits due to cancellation?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: A defer block placed before throwing cancellation checks.
options.explanation: defer blocks execute whenever scope exits, including unwinding from CancellationError.

options.text: An autoreleasepool block surrounding the task declaration.
options.explanation: autoreleasepool manages temporary Objective-C pointers, not task unwinding.

options.text: A fatalError handler registered with the system kernel.
options.explanation: fatalError terminates processes and does not manage normal cleanup.

options.text: A global notification observer listening for app termination.
options.explanation: App termination observers do not manage task-level scope cleanups.

questions.prompt: What does withTaskCancellationHandler do when a task receives cancellation?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: It forces the operation closure to restart on a new worker thread.
options.explanation: withTaskCancellationHandler does not restart operations.

options.text: It executes its onCancel closure immediately upon cancellation.
options.explanation: withTaskCancellationHandler runs the onCancel closure as soon as cancel is requested.

options.text: It converts all thrown errors into non-throwing optional values.
options.explanation: Error handling behavior is determined by whether the operation throws.

options.text: It pauses the canceling thread until the operation closure returns.
options.explanation: onCancel runs immediately and does not pause the canceling thread.

questions.prompt: What concurrency risk exists between operation and onCancel in withTaskCancellationHandler?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: Memory leaks caused by strong reference cycles in the view model.
options.explanation: Reference cycles are an ARC concern, not a concurrency handler race.

options.text: Deadlocks when allocating thread local storage buffers.
options.explanation: Thread local storage does not cause handler race conditions.

options.text: onCancel runs concurrently on the canceling thread, risking data races.
options.explanation: onCancel executes on the thread calling cancel(), which can race with the operation.

options.text: Priority inversions between UI animations and network decoders.
options.explanation: The core hazard of onCancel is concurrent execution with operation.

questions.prompt: How does .task(id: value) in SwiftUI handle task lifetime when value changes?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: It enqueues the new task sequentially after the old task completes.
options.explanation: The modifier does not queue tasks sequentially; it cancels the running task.

options.text: It pauses the current task and resumes it when value returns to original.
options.explanation: Tasks are cancelled and re-created, not paused.

options.text: It ignores the change if the previous task is still downloading.
options.explanation: Value changes trigger cancellation of in-flight work immediately.

options.text: It cancels the in-flight task and restarts a new task with the new value.
options.explanation: .task(id:) cancels existing work when the identity value changes and starts fresh.

questions.prompt: When should you use Task.isCancelled instead of try Task.checkCancellation()?

options.text: In non-throwing functions or when returning partial completed results.
options.explanation: Task.isCancelled is ideal for non-throwing methods or returning partial work.

options.text: When tasks must run with elevated real-time audio thread priority.
options.explanation: Cancellation checks do not alter task priority levels.

options.text: When code must execute exclusively on the main actor thread.
options.explanation: Both checking mechanisms can be used on any actor or thread.

options.text: When launching detached tasks from background GCD dispatch queues.
options.explanation: Task.isCancelled checks cancellation regardless of task structure.

questions.prompt: How does cancellation affect child tasks created with async let?

options.text: async let child tasks ignore parent cancellation entirely.
options.explanation: Structured concurrency guarantees cancellation propagates to async let children.

options.text: Cancellation automatically cascades down to the async let child tasks.
options.explanation: Structured child tasks receive the cancellation flag when the parent task cancels.

options.text: async let child tasks terminate immediately without running defer.
options.explanation: defer blocks always run during scope unwinding in cancelled child tasks.

options.text: async let child tasks switch to running synchronously on the caller thread.
options.explanation: Cancellation does not alter child task thread execution modes.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain why Swift task cancellation is cooperative. What happens if a running loop contains no cancellation checks?

rubric.criterion: Explains that calling cancel() sets a cancellation flag rather than killing threads
Explains that code must inspect Task.isCancelled or checkCancellation to halt work
Explains that a loop without checks will run to completion, wasting CPU and battery

questions.modelAnswer: Swift task cancellation is cooperative because the system sets a cancellation flag instead of killing threads. Running code must explicitly check Task.isCancelled or call try Task.checkCancellation() to stop working. If a running loop contains no cancellation checks, it continues executing until completion, consuming CPU cycles and battery.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, compare Task.isCancelled and try Task.checkCancellation(). Explain when you should choose one over the other.

rubric.criterion: Explains Task.isCancelled returns a Boolean without throwing
Explains try Task.checkCancellation() throws CancellationError
Explains choosing Task.isCancelled for partial returns or non-throwing functions

questions.modelAnswer: Task.isCancelled is a Boolean property that lets you inspect cancellation status without throwing an error. In contrast, try Task.checkCancellation() immediately throws CancellationError if the task is cancelled. You choose Task.isCancelled in non-throwing functions or when returning partial results, and checkCancellation() in throwing asynchronous pipelines.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how the SwiftUI .task modifier handles cancellation automatically. Mention what happens when a view disappears or when an identity value changes.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Explains that .task launches when the view appears and cancels when it disappears
Explains that .task(id:) cancels existing work and restarts when the id value changes
Mentions avoiding manual task cancellation boilerplate in view models

questions.modelAnswer: The SwiftUI .task modifier automatically starts an asynchronous task when the view appears and cancels it when the view disappears. When using .task(id: value), SwiftUI cancels any existing in-flight task whenever the identity value changes, then starts a new one. This handles search-as-you-type cancellations automatically without manual task management.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how withTaskCancellationHandler bridges non-async APIs. What threading hazard must you consider regarding onCancel?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Explains executing an operation while providing an onCancel closure to abort external work
Explains that onCancel runs immediately on whichever thread called cancel()
Identifies data race risks between operation and onCancel requiring synchronization

questions.modelAnswer: withTaskCancellationHandler runs an operation and provides an onCancel closure to cancel legacy resources like network sessions or file descriptors. However, onCancel executes immediately on whatever thread invoked task.cancel(). This means onCancel can run concurrently with the operation, so shared variables must be protected against data races.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how to handle resource cleanups when a task receives cancellation. Why is defer useful in this context?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Explains using defer to guarantee cleanup code runs when scope exits
Explains that defer executes even when checkCancellation throws CancellationError
Mentions cleaning up open handles, sockets, or temporary files

questions.modelAnswer: When a task is cancelled, throwing checkCancellation() unwinds the call stack immediately. Using a defer block ensures cleanup logic always runs regardless of how the function exits. This allows you to close open files, terminate database connections, and release temporary memory safely upon cancellation.
